findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate.
findings.policy_quote: $5,000,000 Each Claim / $5,000,000 Aggregate (per MPLDEC 07 19 Dec page); Excess: $5,000,000 xs $5,000,000 (Convex XPL000040-0425)
findings.policy_page: Gemini Dec page; Convex Dec page (XPL-001 01/24)
findings.policy_file: Redacted2025 - 2026 Professional Liability Policy.pdf + RedactedConvex - 2025-2026 Excess Tech EO Policy.pdf
findings.gap_description: Stated tower of $10M ($5M Gemini primary + $5M Convex excess) materially exceeds the Sacramento County $1M/$1M minimum. Note: this finding addresses the limit-on-paper only — see separate Split Limits tier finding for the practical limit on older Wrongful Acts.
findings.plain_english: On paper your professional liability tower has ten times the coverage Sacramento County requires. Strong limit position — your headline number is well above contract minimum.
findings.recommendation: Maintain current tower. Verify the AM Best rating of Convex Insurance UK Limited meets Sacramento's A-VII threshold (separate finding).

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Split Limits of Liability (Tiered Structure)
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate. ... If professional liability coverage is written on a Claims Made form: A. The 'Retro Date' must be shown, and must be on or before the date of the Agreement or the beginning of Agreement performance by CONTRACTOR.
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #4 (Split Limits of Liability, AD 66 16 04 09) replaces the Limits of Liability section in its entirety with a tiered structure tied to when Wrongful Acts first commenced: (a) Acts on or after Retro Date 12/1/2007: $1M each claim / $1M aggregate; (b) Acts on or after 09/06/2019: additional $1M xs $1M each claim / $1M xs $1M aggregate; (c) Acts on or after 04/01/2021: additional $3M xs $2M each claim / $3M xs $2M aggregate.
findings.gap_description: The full $5M/$5M Gemini primary tower (and the $5M Convex excess that follows form to it) only attaches when the Wrongful Act was first committed on or after 04/01/2021. A claim alleging negligent design, software, ballot processing, or election technology services performed between 12/01/2007 and 09/05/2019 — a 12-year period covering most of Run-Test's recent operational history — is capped at $1M each claim / $1M aggregate. Wrongful Acts between 09/06/2019 and 03/31/2021 are capped at $2M. For an election services firm with 50+ years of operations and long-tail exposure (a 2018 ballot defect could surface today), the disclosed $10M tower is largely illusory. Also flows up to Convex excess via the conditional follow-form clause — Convex follows the more restrictive limits.
findings.plain_english: Your professional liability looks like $10 million on the certificate. In reality, if the alleged error happened before September 2019 — and most of your operational history is before September 2019 — you only have $1 million of coverage available. Election claims often surface years after the fact (a ballot processed in 2018 could be the basis of a 2026 lawsuit). For a 50+ year company in your industry, this tiered structure means most of your historical work is covered at one-tenth the limit you're showing on certificates.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate at next renewal to flatten the Split Limits endorsement and apply the full $5M/$5M to all retro-eligible Wrongful Acts back to 12/01/2007. If the carrier won't flatten, get a written confirmation of which contracts/operations are covered at full limit, and price an excess differences in conditions (DIC) layer that fills the prior-period $4M gap. Disclose the limited-coverage period to the client's General Counsel for litigation/incident-response planning.
discoveryQuestions: If a county sues you in 2026 over a ballot processing issue from the 2018 election cycle, do you know how much of your $10M E&O tower would actually be available to defend and indemnify that claim?
What's the typical latency between a ballot processing error and a county actually filing a claim against your company — months, or years?
When you negotiated this Split Limits structure with the carrier, was the impact on pre-2019 work fully explained, or was it presented as a routine limit endorsement?
How would you describe to your county clients the difference between the $10M limit on your certificate and the $1M limit that actually applies to most of your historical work?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Mail Processing Retro Date Narrowed to 04/01/2021
findings.contract_quote: If professional liability coverage is written on a Claims Made form: A. The 'Retro Date' must be shown, and must be on or before the date of the Agreement or the beginning of Agreement performance by CONTRACTOR.
findings.policy_quote: End. #1 (VP 07 84 07 17 Specific Professional Service Retroactive Date). Retro Date of 04/01/2021 (instead of policy Retro 03/27/2017) applies specifically to 'outbound and inbound mail processing services.'
findings.gap_description: The general retroactive date is 03/27/2017, but a separate, narrower retro of 04/01/2021 has been carved out for outbound/inbound mail processing services — which is one of Run-Test's CORE operations explicitly listed in the Professional Services definition (End. #9). Sacramento County §V.A requires the retro date to be on or before the date of the Agreement or beginning of performance. If Run-Test has been performing mail processing services for any Sacramento agreement that commenced before 04/01/2021, those Wrongful Acts are uncovered. Even for newer contracts, mail processing is the most claim-likely service line — election mail volumes touch tens of millions of voters, deadline-sensitive — and it has the shallowest prior-acts coverage in the entire policy.
findings.plain_english: Mail processing is the work you do that is most likely to generate a lawsuit (ballots not delivered on time, ballots delivered to wrong addresses, etc.) — and it has the SHALLOWEST coverage of all your services. For everything else you do, the policy reaches back to 2017. For mail processing, it only reaches back to April 2021. If a county sues you over mail processing work performed in 2019 or 2020, your E&O policy will refuse the claim outright. This is a coverage carve-out aimed at your most-claimed service line.
findings.recommendation: Request the carrier flatten the mail processing retro to match the general 03/27/2017 retro at next renewal. If carrier insists on keeping it, document for each county contract whether mail processing services pre-04/01/2021 were performed. For the Sacramento agreement specifically, confirm whether contract effective date and beginning of performance both fall on or after 04/01/2021 — if not, this is a contractual non-compliance issue that should be disclosed to the County's Risk Manager.
discoveryQuestions: How long have you been doing inbound and outbound mail processing for your county clients — is any of that work older than April 2021?
When the carrier added a separate, later retro date specifically for mail processing — your most claim-prone service line — was that explained as a coverage reduction or as a routine endorsement?
If a county claim came in tomorrow alleging negligent mail handling in a 2020 election cycle, how would you respond — and have you stress-tested that scenario with your General Counsel?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Maricopa Retro Date Compliance
findings.contract_quote: In the event that the insurance required is written on a claims-made basis, Contractor warrants that any retroactive date under the policy shall precede the effective date of this contract and either continuous coverage will be maintained, or an extended discovery period will be exercised for a period of two years beginning at the time work under this contract is completed.
findings.policy_quote: Retroactive Date 03/27/2017 (Gemini primary); Retroactive Date 03/27/2017 (Convex excess, XPL-502 01/23 End.).
findings.policy_page: Gemini Dec page MPLDEC 07 19; Convex Pg 18 (XPL-502)
findings.policy_file: Redacted2025 - 2026 Professional Liability Policy.pdf + RedactedConvex - 2025-2026 Excess Tech EO Policy.pdf
findings.gap_description: General retro date 03/27/2017 predates the Maricopa contract effective date of 11/01/2021 by 4.5 years. Convex excess matches at 03/27/2017 — no retro gap at the excess layer. Compliant for non-mail-processing Professional Services. Note: see separate finding on the narrower 04/01/2021 mail processing retro, which still predates the 11/01/2021 Maricopa effective date but offers far less prior-acts protection.
findings.plain_english: For everything except mail processing, your retro date is comfortably ahead of the Maricopa contract effective date. The carrier can't refuse a claim on retro grounds for general election services performed at any time during your relationship with Maricopa.
findings.recommendation: Maintain. Confirm the Extended Discovery / ERP availability with Gemini at renewal — Maricopa requires 2-year ERP if coverage is canceled or non-renewed without continuous-retro replacement.

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Extended Reporting Period (ERP) Verification
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §V.B–C: Insurance must be maintained and evidence of insurance must be provided for at least one (1) year after completion of the Agreement... CONTRACTOR must purchase 'extended reporting' coverage for a minimum of one (1) year after completion of the Agreement. Maricopa §8.2.3: ...an extended discovery period will be exercised for a period of two years beginning at the time work under this contract is completed.
findings.policy_quote: ERP availability: not explicitly stated in the Gemini Dec excerpt provided. Convex excess does not contain its own ERP grant — follows form to Gemini.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento County requires a minimum 1-year ERP and Maricopa County requires 2 years if claims-made coverage is canceled or non-renewed without replacement. The Gemini policy includes a Disciplinary Proceeding Coverage Extension (Section II.A) and a Claim Reporting Provision (End. #3, 60-day post-Policy notice) but the standalone Extended Reporting Period grant — its trigger, length, premium, and unilateral availability — is not visible in the extract reviewed. Convex excess follows form. Compliance cannot be confirmed without the full ERP/discovery clause language.
findings.plain_english: If you ever cancel or change carriers on this E&O policy, you may be required to buy a one- or two-year tail (depending on the contract). The cost of that tail and your right to demand it should be confirmed BEFORE you accept a renewal proposal — otherwise you could find yourself contractually obligated to buy something the policy doesn't readily offer.
findings.recommendation: Obtain the Gemini ERP / Extended Reporting Period clause and confirm: (a) is it unilaterally available on demand at any cancellation/non-renewal trigger; (b) what is the length offered (1 yr / 2 yr / 3 yr / 6 yr); (c) what is the premium percentage; (d) is the right tied to specific cancellation reasons or available regardless. Obtain endorsement from Convex confirming excess ERP follows form.

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Client Print Media Exclusion (Election Content From County)
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §III.E and Maricopa §8.2.13 require Professional Liability coverage for the Contractor's services. Election services contracts inherently rely on county-furnished ballot data, voter rolls, and election content provided to the contractor for processing.
findings.policy_quote: End. #5 W. Client Print Media: 'EXCLUDES Claims by clients of the Insured if Claim is a result of print media or Content furnished BY the client.'
findings.gap_description: Counties FURNISH ballot content — candidate names, ballot measures, voter address data, mailing lists, instruction language. Run-Test then prints, processes, and mails based on county-provided content. Endorsement #5 W. expressly excludes Claims by clients arising from print media or Content furnished BY the client. If a county sues Run-Test alleging that printed ballots were defective, miscoded, or contained errors traceable to county-furnished data — even if the actual fault lies with Run-Test's intake/quality-control process — the carrier may invoke this exclusion. This sits at the heart of the contractor's actual risk profile.
findings.plain_english: Your single biggest E&O exposure — a county suing you over a defective ballot run — may be expressly excluded by your policy if the underlying ballot content came from the county. Counties always furnish the candidate list, the measures, the voter file. So when a county comes after you for a problem with what got printed, the carrier could point to this exclusion and walk away. This is a custom-fit exclusion that targets the exact loss scenario your business is most likely to face.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate removal or substantial narrowing of End. #5 W. at next renewal. Alternatives: (a) replace with a 'Negligent Failure to Verify Client-Furnished Content' carve-back; (b) narrow the exclusion to apply only when the Insured had no obligation to verify or proof the content; (c) move primary E&O to a carrier without this exclusion (e.g., Beazley, Berkley/Berkshire, or Lloyd's syndicates that write election technology). Until removed, document — for each county contract — whether intake QC and proofing obligations are explicitly assigned to Run-Test (which would support a 'duty to verify' carve-back argument).
discoveryQuestions: When a county sends you ballot data, what's your QC and proofing process before printing — and does that count as 'verification' of client-furnished content under your contracts?
Has any county client ever blamed a printing or mailing error on your processing of THEIR data — what happened with that claim?
Did your broker explain that the Client Print Media exclusion in your policy could bar coverage for the most common type of claim you'd face — a county suing over content the county itself provided?
What's your understanding of who carries the risk of bad ballot data — the county that provided it, or you for printing what they sent?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Delay in Performance Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate. (Sacramento) ... [implied coverage for time-sensitive election services delivery]
findings.policy_quote: End. #6 D. Delay in Performance/Delivery: 'Excludes delay claims for Technology Products/services/contractual obligations.'
findings.policy_page: Pg 26 of 47 (End. #6 Tech Services Extension D.)
findings.gap_description: Election work is time-CRITICAL by definition. Ballots must be delivered to voters before the registration cut-off, mail-in ballots must be received before deadlines, results must be processed within statutory windows. A delay claim is not a hypothetical — it is the most foreseeable type of claim Run-Test could face. Endorsement #6 D. on the Tech Services Extension expressly excludes claims for delay in performance or delivery of technology products and services. Sublimits or carve-backs do not appear in the extract reviewed.
findings.plain_english: Election deadlines are statutory and don't move. If your delivery is one day late, voters miss the chance to vote — and counties get sued, FEC complaints get filed, and liability flows to you. Your E&O policy says: we don't cover delay claims. The single most foreseeable lawsuit your business could face — 'you delivered the ballots late' — is excluded.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate to remove or carve-back End. #6 D. at next renewal. Acceptable carve-backs would include: (a) coverage for delay caused by Insured's Wrongful Act in design/processing (vs. delay caused by force majeure or third-party logistics); (b) sublimit ($500K–$1M) for delay-induced consequential damages claims; (c) replacement of delay exclusion with a deferral/waiting-period mechanism rather than absolute exclusion. If carrier refuses, evaluate moving primary to a market that does not exclude delay (Beazley Tech & MPL, Lloyd's, BHSI). Cross-check with the Cyber policy's Business Interruption coverage to determine whether there's any backstop for first-party delay losses (third-party delay claims are not covered by Cyber BI).
discoveryQuestions: Walk me through what happens if a Run-Test ballot shipment arrives at a county 24 hours late during an election cycle — who gets sued, and by whom?
Have you ever had a near-miss on an election deadline — a moment where a delay almost happened? What was the cost projection if it had?
When you read 'delay in performance is excluded' — what claim scenario do you think the carrier is contemplating? Does your General Counsel agree with that interpretation?
How would you defend a county's claim that a 12-hour delay in ballot delivery cost them $5M in election remediation costs, given that your E&O carrier won't fund the defense?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Recall / Reprinting Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §III.E and Maricopa §8.2.13 require Professional Liability that responds to errors and omissions in election services.
findings.policy_quote: End. #5 R. Recall/Reprinting: 'Excludes recall, withdrawal, remediation, replacement, or reprinting of print media alleged to cause Media Injury.'
findings.gap_description: If a defective ballot run must be pulled and reprinted — a routine real-world response to a printing error — the cost of the recall and reprint is excluded. The exclusion covers media-injury-related recall but the language ('recall, withdrawal, remediation, replacement, or reprinting') is broad and could apply to mitigation costs that election clients would otherwise expect a competent contractor to absorb under an E&O claim.
findings.plain_english: When a printing error happens, the natural fix is to pull the bad ballots and reprint. That cost — paper, printing, mailing, expedited shipping — could be six- or seven-figures on a county-scale run. Your E&O policy says: that's not our problem. So you eat the reprint costs out of operating margin even when the underlying error is the kind of negligence E&O is supposed to address.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate a sublimit ($250K–$500K) carve-back for mitigation/recall costs at next renewal. Alternatively, evaluate adding a Product Recall / Contamination policy that picks up reprint-style mitigation expenses. Quantify historical reprint cost as part of premium-vs-exposure analysis.
discoveryQuestions: If a printing error required pulling and reprinting a half-million ballots, what would that cost — and where would that money come from in the absence of insurance?
When the carrier explained the Media Extension endorsement, did they highlight that recall and reprint costs were carved out as exclusions?
Have you ever had to do a partial reprint mid-cycle — what was the cost and the source of funds?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Network Security & Privacy Breach Exclusion (Cyber Coordination)
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa §8.2.13 requires Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with $5M limit, and §8.2.13 Professional Liability is separately required (implied per industry standard).
findings.policy_quote: End. #21 (VP 09 97 06 22): excludes from Professional Liability any Claim arising from data breach, network security failure, mishandling of confidential/personal information... Coverage MUST exist on a separate Cyber Coverage Endorsement (or standalone Cyber policy) to cover these exposures.
findings.gap_description: The E&O policy excludes cyber/network security/privacy breach claims to avoid silent-cyber overlap. This is appropriate — these exposures should sit on the dedicated Cyber policy. The program HAS a Cyber policy in place (AmTrust AES1231913 02). The structural separation is correctly designed; the open question (addressed in separate findings) is whether the AmTrust Cyber policy's $4M aggregate, defense-within-limits, shared-aggregate structure, and Cyber Deception phantom sublimit actually provide the coverage that the E&O exclusion presumes.
findings.recommendation: Maintain the structural separation but materially upgrade the Cyber tower (see Cyber findings). The E&O exclusion is fine; the Cyber policy is where the gap actually lives.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: AmTrust Cyber AES1231913 02 (subject to separate findings on cyber adequacy)

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Biometric Identifiers Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §III.E and Maricopa §8.2.13 require Professional Liability coverage for the Contractor's services, which include election authentication technology.
findings.policy_quote: End. #21 (VP 09 97 06 22): 'Excludes any Claim alleging violation of statutes governing collection/use/storage/destruction of biometric identifiers or information' (BIPA-style).
findings.gap_description: Run-Test's products include 'election hardware and software maintenance' (per End. #9 Professional Services definition). Some signature-verification, voter-authentication, or fingerprint-based check-in technology can fall within state biometric statutes (Illinois BIPA, Texas CUBI, Washington biometric law). The exclusion is absolute and removes coverage for any biometric-related statutory violation. The Cyber policy may provide some coverage but biometric exposures are typically excluded or sublimited there too.
findings.plain_english: If any of your election technology touches fingerprints, signature-pattern data, or other biometric ID — even indirectly — and a class action argues you violated state biometric law, both your E&O and likely your Cyber policy will refuse to cover. BIPA cases routinely settle for $10M+. Worth verifying whether your products do or could touch biometrics.
findings.recommendation: First confirm whether Run-Test's election technology products use biometric identifiers in any form. If yes, request a BIPA-specific affirmative grant on either E&O or Cyber, OR purchase a standalone Biometric Liability sublimit. If no biometric use, document that in writing and revisit at any product roadmap change.
discoveryQuestions: Does any of your election technology — voter check-in, signature verification, ballot authentication — capture biometric identifiers like fingerprints or signature patterns?
If your product is deployed in Illinois, Texas, or Washington, do you know how state biometric statutes might apply to election-day data capture?
Has your General Counsel reviewed whether any current product touches biometric data, and what your statutory compliance posture is?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Communicable Disease Absolute Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §III.E and Maricopa §8.2.13 require Professional Liability coverage for the Contractor's services.
findings.policy_quote: End. #20 (VP 09 68 04 20 Communicable Disease Exclusion): 'Absolute exclusion for any Claim alleging/arising out of/attributable to any actual or alleged Communicable Disease — including supervisory/hiring/training acts, testing failures, prevention failures, reporting failures, and related communications.'
findings.gap_description: Post-COVID standard exclusion. Removes coverage for any claim with a communicable disease nexus — including alleged failure to prevent transmission at polling sites, training failures, or election-day public-health protocol failures. For an election services contractor with on-site work at county polling locations, plus mail handling at scale, this could be invoked broadly.
findings.plain_english: If a polling-place outbreak gets traced back to anything you handled — mail, equipment, training — and someone sues, your E&O won't cover it. This is a standard post-pandemic exclusion across the market, but worth knowing.
findings.recommendation: Document the exposure but do not over-prioritize remediation — this is a market-standard exclusion. Confirm communicable disease exclusion is also on the Cyber policy and the (presumed) GL/Umbrella to map the program's overall posture. Workers' Comp picks up employee infection per OSHA/NCCI guidance.
discoveryQuestions: What's your protocol if an outbreak is traced to materials your team handled or distributed during an election cycle?
Have you stress-tested how a public-health-related lawsuit would route through your insurance program — which policy responds, and which exclude it?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — 80/20 Hammer Clause
findings.contract_quote: [Industry standard expectation: insured retains reasonable consent to settle on Professional Liability claims.]
findings.policy_quote: End. #16 (VP 08 51 05 17 Consent to Settle Amendment — Hammer Clause): '80/20 hammer clause — if Named Insured refuses Company's recommended settlement, carrier liability capped at recommended settlement amount + 80% of Claim Expenses and Loss in excess of recommended amount. Insured bears 20%.'
findings.gap_description: Standard 80/20 hammer clause. Materially better than a 100% (full) hammer but more punishing than a 50/50 or pure-consent clause that newer markets offer. If Run-Test refuses to settle a county claim because of reputational/strategic concerns, and the matter eventually resolves above the carrier's recommended figure, the company picks up 20% of the over-spend.
findings.plain_english: If your carrier wants to settle a county lawsuit for $400K and you say 'no, fight it because of reputational impact,' and the case eventually settles or judgments at $1M — you owe 20% of the difference, or $120K. Better than older 'full hammer' clauses but still a real cost of disagreeing with the carrier on settlement strategy. Reputation matters in the elections business — losing a settlement battle on the record can hurt future county RFP wins.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate to a 50/50 hammer or pure consent clause at next renewal. The W.R. Berkley group offers stronger consent provisions on better terms; ask the broker to push. Document for client an internal protocol: if carrier recommends settlement, the C-suite + GC must affirmatively decide to override knowing the 20% co-insurance impact.
discoveryQuestions: Have you ever had a carrier push to settle a claim that you wanted to fight on principle or reputation? How did that play out?

If your E&O carrier recommended settling a county lawsuit for $400K and you wanted to defend through trial because of the reputational implications, are you comfortable with the 20% over-spend on your books?
What's your General Counsel's posture on settlement authority — is it one decision-maker or a committee?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Self-Insured Retention $25,000 Per Claim
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §IV: 'Any deductibles or self-insured retention that apply to any insurance required by this Agreement must be declared and approved by the COUNTY.' Maricopa §8.2.6: 'Such deductible and/or self-insured retentions shall not be applicable with respect to the coverage provided to County under such policies. Contractor shall be solely responsible for the deductible and/or self-insured retention.'
findings.policy_quote: End. #11 (VP 06 99 07 17 Self-Insured Retention): 'Replaces "Deductible" with "Self-Insured Retention" of $25,000 per claim. Insured must pay SIR for both Loss and Claim Expenses BEFORE carrier has any obligation. Carrier has no duty to defend until SIR exhausted.'
findings.gap_description: $25K SIR is modest and within typical range for a $5M tower. SIR must be disclosed to Sacramento per §IV and approved before performance. Maricopa §8.2.6 expressly states the SIR is not applicable to coverage provided to County (i.e., County's defense/indemnity obligation is not eroded by the SIR). Confirm Sacramento has been notified and approved.
findings.plain_english: You self-fund the first $25K of any E&O claim before insurance kicks in — modest and reasonable for a tower this size. Just make sure Sacramento County has been told about the SIR and signed off on it. Maricopa already automatically waives SIR application against the County itself.
findings.recommendation: Pull the Sacramento Risk Manager approval letter (if any) into the file. If not on file, formally disclose the $25K SIR to the County's Risk Manager and request acknowledgment. Document the SIR disclosure on every annual renewal certificate.

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — SIR Defense Obligation Burden on Insured
findings.contract_quote: [Sacramento §V.A–C and Maricopa §8.2.3 contemplate carrier-led defense for claims-made E&O.]
findings.policy_quote: End. #11 (VP 06 99 07 17 SIR): 'Carrier has no duty to defend until SIR exhausted (with right to associate or take over). Insured bears investigation/defense within SIR using Company panel counsel as Claim Service Provider... Insured-retained counsel credited toward SIR but limited to Company's customary hourly rates and counsel must have 10+ years experience and lawyer's PL coverage at least equal to this Policy's limits.'
findings.gap_description: The SIR endorsement is more than a deductible — it shifts the operational burden of defense to the insured for any claim that resolves within the $25K SIR. The insured must use carrier-panel counsel ('Claim Service Provider') OR insured-retained counsel that meets specified experience and PL coverage requirements at carrier's customary hourly rates. Choice-of-counsel constraints can be material in a regulated/elections-litigation context where the insured may want a specific firm experienced in election law.
findings.plain_english: When a claim comes in under $25K, you pay AND you run the defense — but using the carrier's panel of lawyers, or your own lawyer at carrier-set rates and only if they meet experience and PL coverage thresholds. That can be problematic if you have a long-standing relationship with election-law counsel who may not meet the carrier's hourly cap or experience criteria.
findings.recommendation: Identify Run-Test's preferred election-law counsel and confirm whether they qualify under the SIR endorsement criteria (10+ years experience, PL coverage equal to policy limits, willingness to bill at carrier rates). If not, negotiate a counsel-of-choice rider at next renewal or a higher hourly rate cap.
discoveryQuestions: Who's your go-to outside counsel for election-law disputes, and have you confirmed they meet the carrier's panel-counsel criteria for claims under $25K?
On a contested claim that's likely to settle in the $20K range, are you comfortable defending it without carrier involvement?
Has your General Counsel walked through the SIR endorsement and identified any operational friction with how you'd actually want to defend a small claim?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Pending and Prior Litigation Date 03/26/2017
findings.contract_quote: [Standard claims-made underwriting expectation: P&P date well-anchored before contract effective.]
findings.policy_quote: End. #18 (VP 02 89 10 17 Pending and Prior Litigation Exclusion with Date): 'P&P Litigation Date: 3/26/2017.'
findings.gap_description: P&P date is well anchored before any current Sacramento or Maricopa contract effective date. No coverage gap from this exclusion for present-day operations. Long-standing carrier relationship preserved consistent retro/P&P dates over multiple renewals.
findings.recommendation: Maintain. Verify P&P date is preserved at each renewal — do not allow it to shift forward.

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Surplus Lines / Non-Admitted Carrier in Arizona
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §VI.A.1: 'Insurance is to be placed with insurers with a current A.M. Best's rating of no less than A-VII.' Maricopa §8.2.1: 'a company or companies duly licensed by the State of Arizona and possessing an AM Best, Inc. category rating of B++.'
findings.policy_quote: Gemini Insurance Company (a Delaware Stock Company; W.R. Berkley group; non-admitted in Arizona — surplus lines)
findings.gap_description: Gemini Insurance Company is a W.R. Berkley group company. AM Best typically rates W.R. Berkley group A+ (Superior) with size category XV — comfortably exceeding both Sacramento A-VII and Maricopa B++ thresholds. However, the AM Best rating must be confirmed in writing on the COI annually. Sacramento additionally requires the carrier be 'placed with' an A-VII-rated insurer; Maricopa allows non-admitted if Arizona-licensed surplus lines compliant. Tech E&O for election services is appropriately placed in the surplus lines market — admitted carriers rarely write this risk class.
findings.recommendation: Pull current AM Best rating for Gemini Insurance Company directly from AM Best (do not rely on broker certification alone). Confirm both rating tier (A- or better) and size category (VII or better). Update broker records and COI templates with current rating annually. Note: surplus lines placement itself is appropriate per KB Rule 15.

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Convex Excess Conditional Follow-Form Trap
findings.contract_quote: [Industry standard expectation: excess layer should not be more restrictive than primary unless explicitly noted.]
findings.policy_quote: XPL-300 §I: 'If any Underlying Policy includes any more restrictive coverage, terms, definitions, exclusions, conditions, or limitations, then this policy will follow the more restrictive provisions of any Underlying Policy.'
findings.gap_description: Conditional follow-form means every restrictive endorsement on Gemini primary (Split Limits tier, Mail Processing retro carve-out, Client Print Media exclusion, Delay exclusion, Recall exclusion, Biometric exclusion, Communicable Disease exclusion, Hammer clause, Network Security/Privacy Breach exclusion) flows up to the Convex excess. The $5M xs $5M tower offers no broader coverage than Gemini primary — every primary restriction caps the excess identically. If a claim is excluded on Gemini, it is excluded on Convex. The Split Limits tier cap on pre-09/2019 acts therefore caps the entire $10M tower at $1M for those Wrongful Acts.
findings.plain_english: Your $5M excess layer has all the same exclusions as your primary. Every problem with the underlying policy carries up to the excess. If a claim is denied on the primary because of the Client Print Media exclusion, the excess is denied for the same reason. You don't get a 'second look' from a different carrier — you get a $5M layer with identical defects.
findings.recommendation: At next renewal, evaluate whether to: (a) replace Convex with a true 'broader-than-primary' Difference-in-Conditions excess that affirmatively grants coverage on at least the most material primary exclusions (Client Print Media, Delay, Split Limits tier); (b) negotiate concurrent removal/narrowing of primary exclusions to reduce the harm; (c) ladder a third-layer over the program from a market that breaks form (e.g., Lloyd's-led DIC layer). Document the conditional follow-form impact for the C-suite.
discoveryQuestions: When you bought the $5M Convex excess layer, was it presented as broader coverage or as identical-form-but-higher-limit?
If your primary E&O denies a claim using the Client Print Media or Delay exclusion, do you understand that your excess will deny it for the same reason?
Has any broker or carrier offered to write a Difference-in-Conditions layer that would actually pick up exclusions in the primary?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Convex Sublimits Not Extended
findings.contract_quote: [Industry standard expectation: excess layer extends primary coverage at full limits.]
findings.policy_quote: XPL-300 §II: 'If any Underlying Policy grants coverage subject to a sublimit of liability, this policy shall not afford such coverage, however this policy shall recognize any reduction or exhaustion of the Attachment Point by payments with respect to such coverage pursuant to that Underlying Policy.'
findings.gap_description: Any sublimited coverage on Gemini primary (Disciplinary Proceeding $25K/$50K, Subpoena Response $2.5K/$5K, Supplementary Payments wage-loss $250/day-$5K) is not extended by the Convex excess — but those sublimit payments DO erode the $5M attachment. So the insured pays for sublimited coverage twice (no excess available) but still depletes the underlying.
findings.plain_english: If a Disciplinary Proceeding eats $50K of your primary, the $5M excess won't pick it up — and you've still burned $50K of your underlying capacity. Standard for follow-form excess policies, but worth understanding when modeling claim-cost scenarios.
findings.recommendation: Document the sublimit gap. Quantify expected sublimit erosion impact. At next renewal, consider negotiating that high-frequency sublimits (Disciplinary, Subpoena) be paid outside the limits at primary level so they don't deplete the attachment point.
discoveryQuestions: How frequently does Run-Test face disciplinary proceedings or subpoena responses tied to election work — annually, or rare?
Have you ever exhausted a primary sublimit and found that the excess didn't pick up the difference?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Convex Maintenance of Underlying (Favorable Construction)
findings.contract_quote: [Industry best practice: maintenance failure should not void excess coverage entirely.]
findings.policy_quote: XPL-300 §IV.D: 'If insured fails to maintain underlying or renews/replaces with lesser coverage, Convex is liable only as if the underlying had been fully maintained. Failure to maintain does NOT void the policy.'
findings.gap_description: This is the FAVORABLE construction of the maintenance-of-underlying clause. If primary lapses or shrinks, Convex still attaches at the original $5M attachment point — insured eats the gap between actual and presumed underlying, but coverage is not voided wholesale. The unfavorable alternative (used by some umbrellas) is 'failure to maintain voids excess entirely.' Convex's drafting here is a meaningful credit.
findings.plain_english: If your primary E&O lapses or you replace it with a smaller policy, the excess still works — you just plug the gap between what the primary should be and what it actually is. Better than the kind of excess policy that becomes worthless if the primary lapses.
findings.recommendation: Maintain. Confirm at each renewal that this clause is unchanged.

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Convex Drop-Down for Uncollectability Excluded
findings.contract_quote: [Best-practice expectation: excess drops down for primary insolvency.]
findings.policy_quote: XPL-300 §II: 'The risk of uncollectability with respect to any Underlying Policy or Underlying Insurers for any reason is expressly retained by the Insured and is not covered under this policy.'
findings.gap_description: If Gemini Insurance Company becomes insolvent or fails to pay, Convex does NOT drop down to fill the primary $5M layer. Insured retains the full uncollectability risk. Mitigated by: (a) Gemini is W.R. Berkley group (financially strong, A+ AM Best); (b) Gemini is non-admitted in AZ so no AZ Guaranty Fund backstop. Likelihood of Gemini insolvency low but not zero.
findings.plain_english: If your primary carrier goes broke, your excess won't fill the hole. You'd be a creditor in the primary's liquidation. Low probability but unlimited impact.
findings.recommendation: Document. Re-rate Gemini's financial strength annually via AM Best. If rating ever drops to A- or below, immediately evaluate replacement of primary. Consider whether the broker can negotiate a drop-down endorsement on Convex (rare but available) for the next renewal.
discoveryQuestions: Do you monitor your carriers' AM Best ratings annually, and is there a trigger that would cause you to replace a carrier whose rating drops?
If Gemini went insolvent tomorrow, what's your plan for the $5M primary layer of E&O coverage?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Convex Duty to Defend Drop-Down When Underlying Exhausted
findings.contract_quote: [Best-practice expectation: excess assumes defense when primary exhausted.]
findings.policy_quote: XPL-300 §IV.B.2: 'We will have the right and duty to defend any claim made or suit brought or proceeding instituted against an Insured to which this policy applies if the applicable limits of Underlying Policies have been exhausted.'
findings.gap_description: When primary $5M is exhausted, Convex affirmatively takes on the duty to defend. Strong provision — many excess forms only grant 'right' to defend, not 'duty.' Material in catastrophic-claim scenarios where primary exhausts on a still-pending matter.
findings.recommendation: Maintain. Confirm at each renewal.

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Convex Policy Number Discrepancy
findings.contract_quote: [Industry standard: schedule of underlying must accurately reference the primary policy.]
findings.policy_quote: Convex Dec page Item 5 shows Gemini policy VIPL056495; Schedule of Underlying Insurance (XPL-301, page 13) shows VIPL055885. Both Gemini, but the policy number doesn't match.
findings.gap_description: Administrative defect: the Convex Dec Item 5 references Gemini VIPL056495; the underlying schedule references VIPL055885. Both are Gemini policy numbers — likely a renewal-vs-prior-term policy number with a clerical error. Could be argued by carrier in a coverage dispute that the excess policy responds only to the policy number named in the Schedule. Easy fix; meaningful if a claim is contested.
findings.plain_english: There's a clerical mismatch between which underlying policy your excess says it's stacking on top of. In a claim dispute, that mismatch could be used as a technical hook. Easy to fix — request a corrected endorsement from Convex.
findings.recommendation: Request a correcting endorsement from Convex confirming the Schedule of Underlying Insurance is updated to match the current Gemini policy number (VIPL056495). 5-minute fix that closes a 5-year exposure.
discoveryQuestions: Has your broker scrubbed the Schedule of Underlying on the Convex excess against the current Gemini policy number?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Convex AM Best Rating Verification
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §VI.A.1 A-VII; Maricopa §8.2.1 B++.
findings.policy_quote: Convex Insurance UK Limited (surplus lines / non-admitted in AZ); UK PRA/FCA-regulated subsidiary of Convex Re (Bermuda parent).
findings.gap_description: AM Best rates Convex Group on a group basis; recent rating is typically A- (Excellent) with size category in mid-tier. Need to verify the CURRENT rating against Sacramento's A-VII and Maricopa's B++ thresholds at the legal-entity level (Convex Insurance UK Limited specifically). Surplus lines placement is appropriate for $5M xs $5M Tech E&O — admitted markets do not write this risk class at this layer for election services firms.
findings.recommendation: Pull current AM Best rating for Convex Insurance UK Limited (not just the Group) from AM Best directly. Confirm A- or better and size VII or better. If the rating is below either threshold, request waiver from Sacramento Risk Manager (allowed under §VI.A.1) and document Maricopa acknowledgment.

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Maricopa $5M Per-Occurrence Limit Shortfall
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence. The policy shall include, but not be limited to; coverage for all directors, officers, agents and employees of the Contractor, losses with respect to network risks (such as data breaches, unauthorized access or use, and ID theft of data), invasion of privacy (regardless of the type of media involved in the loss of private information), crisis management, identity theft response costs, breach notification costs, credit remediation, and credit monitoring, defense, and claims expenses, regulatory defense costs plus fines and penalties, cyber extortion, electronic data restoration expenses (data asset protection), network business interruption, computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction, and loss outside the premises of the named insured.
findings.policy_quote: Aggregate Limit of Liability: $4,000,000. DEFENSE COSTS ARE PART OF AND NOT IN ADDITION TO THE AGGREGATE LIMIT OF LIABILITY. THE AGGREGATE LIMIT OF LIABILITY AVAILABLE TO PAY LOSS AND THE RETENTION SHALL BE REDUCED AND MAY BE EXHAUSTED BY THE PAYMENT OF DEFENSE COSTS.
findings.gap_description: TRIPLE FAILURE: (1) Maricopa requires $5M per occurrence; AmTrust provides $4M aggregate (not per-occurrence) — direct shortfall of $1M+ on stated limit. (2) Defense Within Limits erodes the aggregate; cyber claims typically consume 60–80% of recovery on forensics, breach counsel, PR, and regulatory defense, leaving effective indemnity of $800K–$1.6M. (3) The aggregate is shared across 14 coverage lines. A single $2M ransomware leaves only $2M of capacity for any subsequent BI, regulatory defense, payment card claim, etc. for the rest of the policy year. No excess Cyber tower exists in the program. This is a direct, material, uncured contractual breach as of policy inception 04/01/2025.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa's contract requires $5M of cyber coverage. You have $4M — and that $4M shrinks every time the lawyers bill, every time you pay a forensic firm, every time PR sends an invoice. By the time a real cyber claim plays out, you may have $1M of actual indemnity available. For a company that touches data on 90 million voters across 31 states, this is dangerously thin. And it's a contractual breach with Maricopa County right now — they could declare you in default if they ever audit your COI/policy.
findings.recommendation: URGENT: increase Cyber primary to at least $5M dedicated aggregate AND/OR ladder a $5M xs $4M Excess Cyber from a market with broader form (Beazley, Coalition, Resilience, At-Bay, or AXIS). Concurrently: (1) negotiate Defense-Outside-Limits on the new layer; (2) replace shared-aggregate structure with line-of-business-specific sublimits at the primary; (3) verify the Cyber Deception sublimit becomes a meaningful number (see separate finding); (4) pre-disclose the in-flight remediation to Maricopa Risk Management to reduce default exposure.
discoveryQuestions: When the Maricopa contract was signed in 2021 with a $5M cyber requirement, who at Run-Test verified that the cyber policy actually met that limit — and has anyone reverified each year since?

Walk me through what happens if a ransomware actor encrypts your election technology platform 30 days before a federal election cycle — what's your forensics plus breach counsel plus business interruption cost trajectory in the first 60 days?

Does your General Counsel know that defense costs under your cyber policy reduce the indemnity available — and that on a typical breach, the lawyers eat 60–80% of the limit before you see a dollar of actual loss recovery?
Have you ever been asked by a county client to provide proof that your cyber limit actually meets the contract minimum, or is it accepted on the strength of the certificate alone?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Cyber Deception / Social Engineering Phantom Coverage
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence. The policy shall include, but not be limited to;... computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction, and loss outside the premises of the named insured.
findings.policy_quote: Cyber Deception / Social Engineering: Limit $250,000 / Retention $250,000. Effective recoverable on any single loss is $0; on a $500K loss the recovery is capped at $250K (50%).
findings.gap_description: PHANTOM COVERAGE: the $250K limit equals the $250K retention. On any single loss, the effective recoverable is ZERO. A $300K social engineering wire transfer fraud yields $50K of recovery. A $500K loss yields $250K (50% loss recovery). Run-Test handles county invoicing, vendor payables, and regulated election-services payments — the social engineering / business email compromise (BEC) attack vector is the single most likely cyber-financial loss it will face. Maricopa §8.2.13 requires computer fraud, funds transfer loss, and third-party fidelity coverage. Calling this 'coverage' is generous — the structure provides effectively zero indemnity.
findings.plain_english: If your AP team gets tricked by a fake email and wires $400,000 to a fraudulent vendor account, your cyber policy will pay you $150,000 — $400K loss minus $250K retention. If the loss is $250,000 or less, you get nothing. This isn't insurance — it's a marketing line on the dec page. Your single most likely cyber dollar-loss is structurally uncovered, and Maricopa's contract specifically calls out this coverage as required.
findings.recommendation: URGENT: at the time of cyber tower upgrade (see finding-024), demand a Cyber Deception / Social Engineering sublimit of at least $1M with a $25K-$50K retention (NOT a retention equal to the limit). Coalition, At-Bay, Beazley, and Resilience all offer 7-figure SE limits with reasonable retentions. As an interim control: implement dual-approval wire transfer protocols, callback verification, and AP fraud training — these reduce frequency until the policy is upgraded.
discoveryQuestions: How does your AP team handle a vendor banking change request — is there a callback protocol, dual approval, or both?
Has any Runbeck employee ever received a phishing email impersonating a county finance director or vendor — what was the response?
Did anyone explain that the $250K Cyber Deception limit is effectively zero because the retention equals the limit?
What's your single largest payable cycle — annual peak or election-cycle peak — and how does that compare to the $250K phantom limit?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Defense Within Limits + Shared Aggregate Combined Effect
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence. The policy shall include... defense, and claims expenses, regulatory defense costs plus fines and penalties...
findings.policy_quote: DEFENSE COSTS ARE PART OF AND NOT IN ADDITION TO THE AGGREGATE LIMIT OF LIABILITY. THE AGGREGATE LIMIT OF LIABILITY AVAILABLE TO PAY LOSS AND THE RETENTION SHALL BE REDUCED AND MAY BE EXHAUSTED BY THE PAYMENT OF DEFENSE COSTS. (Plus shared aggregate across 14 coverage lines.)
findings.gap_description: Combined effect: $4M cap × 14 lines × DWL erosion = effective indemnity per claim of $800K–$1.6M against a $5M Maricopa contract minimum. A single ransomware-plus-class-action could exhaust the aggregate inside the policy year on defense alone. This is not 'a finding requiring further analysis' — it is a structural inadequacy for a vendor with election-cycle peak periods, regulated data, and 31-state operating footprint.
findings.plain_english: The defense lawyers, forensic investigators, and PR firms eat your policy from the inside. By the time you have an actual loss to claim, the limit has already been substantially depleted. Combined with the shared aggregate across 14 coverage types, one bad year means the policy is effectively gone before the second incident hits.
findings.recommendation: Replace at next renewal with a Cyber program that has Defense Outside Limits OR a separate Defense Cost Allowance, plus dedicated per-line sublimits with their own caps (not shared with the master aggregate). This is industry-standard for sophisticated cyber programs at this revenue tier; AmTrust's product is structured for smaller risks.
discoveryQuestions: If you had two cyber events in a single year — say a Q1 ransomware and a Q3 data breach — would your $4M policy aggregate even cover the first, let alone the second?
What's your modeled cost of a 60-day breach response: forensics + counsel + PR + notification + credit monitoring + regulatory defense?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Continuity Date 04/01/2023 vs 50+ Year Operating History
findings.contract_quote: In the event that the insurance required is written on a claims-made basis, Contractor warrants that any retroactive date under the policy shall precede the effective date of this contract and either continuous coverage will be maintained, or an extended discovery period will be exercised for a period of two years beginning at the time work under this contract is completed.
findings.policy_quote: Continuity Date: 4/1/2023 (Item 5 of CYDECS 0122 Dec page)
findings.gap_description: Maricopa contract effective 11/01/2021. Cyber Continuity Date 04/01/2023 is AFTER the contract effective date. Any breach where the unauthorized access began before 04/01/2023 — including a persistent threat actor with an established foothold dating back further — would not be covered. Run-Test has 50+ years of operations and continuous IT systems; the 2-year continuity is materially inadequate. Maricopa §8.2.3 requires retro to precede contract effective date — this is a non-compliance issue.
findings.plain_english: Your cyber policy only goes back to April 2023. Your contract with Maricopa goes back to November 2021. If an attacker has been quietly camped in your systems since 2022, the carrier could refuse the claim on continuity grounds — and Maricopa's contract is technically in breach because the retro doesn't go back to contract effective. Persistent-threat-actor scenarios in the elections sector are increasingly common.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate Continuity Date back to at least 11/01/2021 (Maricopa contract effective) at next renewal — ideally back to the inception of any prior cyber policy held by Run-Test. If AmTrust will not extend, replace primary with a market that will (Beazley, Coalition). Document: pull every county contract effective date and confirm Continuity Date precedes the earliest. Disclose the gap to Maricopa Risk Management proactively to reduce default risk.
discoveryQuestions: When did Run-Test first purchase cyber insurance — and is the current continuity date matching the inception of your earliest cyber program?
How long have your election technology platforms been continuously operating, and does your IT team have evidence of when they were last fully audited for advanced persistent threats?
Were Maricopa's pre-November-2021 contract years consciously discussed when accepting an April 2023 continuity date?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Additional Insured Status (Maricopa Required)
findings.contract_quote: The insurance policies required by this contract, except Workers' Compensation and Errors and Omissions, shall name County, its agents, representatives, officers, directors, officials, and employees as additional insureds.
findings.policy_quote: Item 8 Endorsements list shows blank in extracted text; no AI endorsement visible on Cyber.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.7 carve-out excludes WC and E&O from the AI requirement — but NOT Cyber. The contract therefore expressly requires the Cyber policy to name County and its representatives as additional insureds. No AI endorsement is visible on the AmTrust Cyber policy. Note: many cyber forms structurally do not accommodate AI status because the cyber loss is the insured's loss (first-party) rather than a third-party claim where AI status would normally attach. Carrier may not write the endorsement at all. Either way, the contractual breach exists and must be addressed (either by amending the contract, getting carrier acknowledgment, or moving to a market that will endorse).
findings.plain_english: Maricopa's contract requires the County to be added as an additional insured on your cyber policy. That endorsement is not on the policy — and many cyber carriers won't even write it. Either the contract needs a written exception from Maricopa Risk Management, or the policy needs to move to a carrier that will endorse, or both. Right now, you're in technical breach.
findings.recommendation: Three-path remediation: (1) Request AmTrust endorsement adding Maricopa County as AI on Cyber — if granted, attach to next COI; (2) If AmTrust declines, request written waiver from Maricopa County Risk Manager acknowledging the cyber-AI gap and accepting the program structure; (3) At next renewal, prefer a cyber market that does endorse AI (Beazley, Coalition support broader scheduled-AI). Document all three pathways before declaring compliance.
discoveryQuestions: Has AmTrust ever responded to an AI request on your Cyber policy, and is there documented evidence one way or the other?
Have any other county clients asked for AI status on your cyber policy — and how did you handle it?
Would Maricopa Risk Management be open to a written waiver acknowledging that cyber AI is a market limitation?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Waiver of Subrogation (Maricopa Required)
findings.contract_quote: The policies required hereunder, except Workers' Compensation and Errors and Omissions, shall contain a waiver of transfer of rights of recovery (subrogation) against County, its agents, representatives, officers, directors, officials, and employees for any claims arising out of Contractor's work or service.
findings.policy_quote: No WoS endorsement visible on the AmTrust Cyber policy. Item 8 Endorsements list blank in extract.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.8 carve-out excludes WC and E&O from WoS — but NOT Cyber. Required WoS endorsement absent. If a cyber loss is caused or contributed to by a county employee's actions (e.g., County IT staff accessing Run-Test systems), AmTrust could subrogate against the County after paying Run-Test, putting Run-Test in breach of its contractual obligation to ensure no such recourse.
findings.plain_english: Your cyber policy must waive its right to come after Maricopa County after paying you for a loss. That waiver isn't on the policy. If your insurer pays a claim and then sues the County to get the money back — and the contract said you'd prevent that — Maricopa can come after you to make them whole.
findings.recommendation: Request AmTrust endorse a Blanket Waiver of Subrogation in favor of any party where required by written contract. If AmTrust doesn't offer it on Cyber, escalate or consider replacement at renewal. Confirm in writing with carrier the WoS application across all 14 sublimited coverage lines.
discoveryQuestions: Has AmTrust confirmed in writing whether they will issue a Blanket Waiver of Subrogation on the Cyber policy?

If a county IT employee's negligence contributed to a Run-Test breach, do you understand that the carrier could pay you and then sue Maricopa — and that Maricopa's contract makes you the backstop for that?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Primary & Noncontributory (Maricopa Required)
findings.contract_quote: Contractor's insurance shall be primary insurance as respects County, and any insurance or self-insurance maintained by County shall not contribute to it.
findings.policy_quote: No P&NC endorsement visible on AmTrust Cyber. Item 8 Endorsements list blank.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.4 applies P&NC to all required policies — including Cyber. The endorsement is not visible on the AmTrust Cyber policy. Less critical than AI/WoS because P&NC primarily affects the priority of coverage if County also has cyber insurance — but contract still requires it.
findings.plain_english: If both your cyber policy and the County's cyber policy could respond, Maricopa's contract says yours has to go first. The endorsement that confirms that priority isn't on your policy.
findings.recommendation: Request AmTrust endorse Primary & Noncontributory on the Cyber policy at next quarterly servicing or at renewal — for AI parties (i.e., Maricopa). Standalone endorsement or as part of an AI endorsement.
discoveryQuestions: Does your broker have a documented endorsement-package request out to AmTrust covering AI + WoS + P&NC?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Designated Entity NOC / 30-Day Cancellation Notice (Maricopa Required)
findings.contract_quote: Applicable to all insurance policies required within the insurance requirements of this contract, Contractor's insurance shall not be permitted to expire, be suspended, be canceled, or be materially changed for any reason without 30 days prior written notice to Maricopa County. Contractor must provide to Maricopa County, within two business days of receipt, if they receive notice of a policy that has been or will be suspended, canceled, materially changed for any reason, has expired, or will be expiring.
findings.policy_quote: No Designated Entity NOC endorsement visible. Cancellation notice provisions not visible in 4-page Dec excerpt.
findings.policy_page: Pg 4 of 4 (Item 8 endorsements blank in extract)
findings.gap_description: Maricopa requires 30-day prior written notice of cancellation/material change ON the policy itself (not just Contractor pass-through) for ALL required policies, which includes Cyber per §8.2.13. The standard ACORD COI cancellation language is insufficient — Maricopa's drafting requires the carrier to actually provide notice. No Designated Entity NOC endorsement appears on the Cyber. Contract is in technical breach.
findings.plain_english: If AmTrust cancels your Cyber policy mid-term, Maricopa's contract requires they give the County 30 days' notice. Without the right endorsement, the carrier has no obligation to do that. You're contractually responsible for an obligation your carrier hasn't agreed to.
findings.recommendation: Request AmTrust endorse a Designated Entity NOC (typically a manuscript endorsement on cyber forms) naming Maricopa County as an entity entitled to 30-day prior cancellation/material-change notice. If AmTrust does not offer such an endorsement, request a carrier letter confirming notice procedures and disclose to Maricopa Risk Management. Same evaluation needs to happen on every required policy in the program.
discoveryQuestions: If AmTrust sent a non-renewal notice tomorrow, who at Run-Test would send the 30-day pass-through notice to Maricopa Risk Management — and is that a documented protocol?
Has any policy in the program been canceled or non-renewed mid-term, and if so what was the County notification process?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Proof of Loss Sublimit Inadequate
findings.contract_quote: [Maricopa §8.2.13 requires comprehensive cyber coverage including business interruption — proof-of-loss is a necessary mechanic to claim BI.]
findings.policy_quote: Proof of Loss sublimit: Limit $250,000 / Retention $50,000.
findings.gap_description: Forensic accounting required to prove a Business Interruption claim of any meaningful size against a $5M-$25M revenue contractor would routinely exceed $200K — particularly in election-cycle BI scenarios involving lost mail processing throughput, contract re-bid costs, and vendor displacement. The $250K cap with $50K retention provides $200K of net forensic-accounting allowance against potentially multi-million-dollar BI claims.
findings.plain_english: When you make a business interruption claim, you have to PROVE the loss — and that means hiring forensic accountants. Your policy gives you $200K of net coverage for that work. On a multi-million-dollar BI claim, forensic accounting alone can run $400K–$700K. You'd be paying half the proof-up bill out of pocket.
findings.recommendation: Request a higher Proof of Loss sublimit ($500K–$1M) at the cyber tower upgrade. As an interim, have the broker confirm whether the $250K is INSIDE or OUTSIDE the master aggregate (likely shares the aggregate, which compounds the inadequacy).
discoveryQuestions: If a 60-day BI event happened during peak election season, what's your modeled lost revenue — and how much forensic accounting work would proving that take?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Regulatory Defense Costs Plus Fines and Penalties Coverage Verification
findings.contract_quote: ...regulatory defense costs plus fines and penalties...
findings.policy_quote: Regulatory Fines and Penalties: Limit $4,000,000 / Retention $50,000 (per Dec page sublimit schedule).
findings.gap_description: The Dec page lists 'Regulatory Fines and Penalties' as a sublimit at the master limit. Maricopa's contract specifically requires 'regulatory defense costs PLUS fines and penalties' — meaning fines and penalties must be insurable, not just defense costs. The actual coverage form language (CYCG, CY supplements) is needed to confirm: (a) fines/penalties are affirmatively insured (not just defense); (b) fines/penalties are insured 'where insurable by law' — which is the standard carve-back; (c) the $4M sublimit is shared with the master aggregate (which it appears to be) or stand-alone.
findings.recommendation: Pull the full coverage form from AmTrust and confirm fines-and-penalties insurability language. Identify which jurisdictions allow fines/penalties to be insured (varies by state and statute — most consumer-protection and HIPAA fines allow it; some FTC penalties don't) and overlay against Run-Test's 31-state operating footprint. Confirm sublimit position against master aggregate. If language is restrictive, address at cyber tower upgrade.

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Regulatory Fines/Penalties + Election Cyber Statutes (CISA, State)
findings.contract_quote: ...regulatory defense costs plus fines and penalties...
findings.policy_quote: Regulatory Fines and Penalties: Limit $4,000,000 / Retention $50,000 (shared aggregate); Privacy & Network Security: $4M shared aggregate.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test serves election infrastructure designated as critical infrastructure under the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). The Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act (CIRCIA) imposes mandatory 72-hour reporting requirements; state election integrity statutes can impose further disclosure obligations. Regulatory exposure for Run-Test is unique and potentially expensive (federal, state, multiple counties simultaneously). $4M shared aggregate may be exhausted by regulatory defense alone in a multi-jurisdictional incident.
findings.plain_english: Election infrastructure is federal critical infrastructure under CISA. A breach involving voter data could trigger 31 state attorneys general, federal regulators, and DOJ all at once. Your $4M shared aggregate could be eaten by defense costs alone before you cover any fines, notification, or remediation.
findings.recommendation: At cyber upgrade, ensure dedicated regulatory defense + fines sublimit (separate from the master aggregate) of at least $5M, with multi-jurisdictional defense capacity. Specifically negotiate language addressing CISA/CIRCIA reporting and election-specific state statutes.
discoveryQuestions: Are you currently subject to CISA/CIRCIA 72-hour cyber incident reporting obligations as a designated critical infrastructure vendor?
Has your General Counsel mapped state-level election security statutes against your operating footprint — and do you have a coordinated multi-state regulatory defense playbook?
If a breach triggered simultaneous AG investigations in 31 states plus a federal probe, what's your modeled defense cost — and how does that compare to your $4M aggregate?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Choice of Law New York for Arizona-Domiciled Insured
findings.contract_quote: [Industry standard expectation: choice of law aligns with insured's domicile or principal place of business.]
findings.policy_quote: Choice of Law: New York.

findings.requirement_type: Cross-Program — Tail / ERP Coverage on Claims-Made Cyber
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa §8.2.3 requires 2-year ERP for claims-made policies if not continuously renewed.
findings.policy_quote: AmTrust Cyber: 'Extended Discovery Period offered: 1 Year at 100% of Annual Premium.'
findings.gap_description: AmTrust Cyber offers ONE year of Extended Discovery at 100% of annual premium. Maricopa requires TWO years of discovery period. Direct non-compliance if policy is canceled or non-renewed without continuous-retro replacement. The 100% premium cost for a 1-year tail is also above-market — typical cyber tails are 100-150% for 12 months, 175-250% for 24 months.
findings.plain_english: If you cancel or replace your cyber policy, the carrier will only sell you a 1-year tail. Maricopa's contract requires 2 years. So if you ever change cyber carriers, you immediately become non-compliant with Maricopa unless the new carrier accepts your old retro date — which is unlikely without a coverage gap.
findings.recommendation: Address at cyber tower replacement (see finding-024). New cyber carrier should: (a) accept retro back to 11/1/2021 minimum; (b) offer 24-month ERP at reasonable premium; (c) match continuity date to prior cyber inception. As an interim, request AmTrust offer a 24-month ERP option.

findings.policy_quote: Convex is a dedicated EXCESS PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY policy specifically following form to Gemini primary E&O — NOT a commercial umbrella. The Sacramento §II.E exclusion is aimed at commercial umbrellas being used to satisfy the PL minimum, not at dedicated PL excess towers.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento §II.E is satisfied: the Sacramento $1M/$1M PL minimum is met by Gemini primary alone ($5M, comfortably exceeding the minimum). The Convex excess is a permissible vehicle for stacking on the E&O tower because it is a dedicated PL excess, not a commercial umbrella. Compliant.
findings.recommendation: Maintain. Document the structural distinction in the audit deliverable so this is not misread as non-compliance.

findings.gap_description: TOP THREE PROGRAMMATIC PRIORITIES IN ORDER OF URGENCY: (1) CYBER TOWER UPGRADE — replace AmTrust $4M with $5M-$10M tower at carrier with broader form, fix Cyber Deception phantom coverage, fix Maricopa AI/WoS/P&NC/NOC compliance gaps, fix Continuity Date back to 11/1/2021 minimum (findings 024–031, 088, 095). (2) PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY SPLIT-LIMITS REMEDIATION — flatten the Split Limits tier to apply full $5M/$5M tower across all retro-eligible Wrongful Acts back to 12/01/2007, OR add DIC layer for the prior-period gap; concurrently address Mail Processing retro and Client Print Media exclusion as the highest-impact form defects (findings 002, 003, 006, 007). (3) NAMED INSURED ENTITY-TYPE CORRECTION — fix the Inc/LLC asymmetry across the program using the same template AmTrust used in April 2025 (finding 044). These three remediation tracks address roughly 80% of the program's quantifiable risk-weighted exposure.
findings.plain_english: If you do nothing else from this audit, do these three things: (1) Fix your cyber tower — it's structurally inadequate and you're already in technical breach with Maricopa. (2) Fix the split-limits trap on your professional liability — your $10M tower only provides $1M for most of your historical work. (3) Fix your company name across the rest of your policies — Inc vs LLC. Together, these are the difference between a defensible insurance program and one that fails when you actually need it.
findings.recommendation: Schedule three separate working sessions with C-suite + GC + broker over the next 90 days, each devoted to one of the three remediation tracks. Each session produces a written remediation plan with owner, timeline, and budget. Reconvene for a final program review before the next renewal cycle (currently 4/1/2026 for cyber and PL).
